title: Every visual difference carries a stated meaning
statement: Give every visual difference on screen a meaning and a key, or drop it, and never let one look, such as a highlight colour, stand for two things.
example: One word web styled all 6 of its words alike while its line told learners some were new and some they brought with them.
detail: The review of a Grade 9 prototype's word web found an unexplained dotted line between two words and judged that a dotted line carrying meaning needs a key, and one carrying none should not look different (`g9/library/text/L36b8ba.txt`, line 228). The same screen told learners that some words were their own and some new while all six nodes were styled identically (line 228). Its build items style the learner's own words differently, so the line is true on screen, and give the dotted line a key or make it solid (lines 84 and 86).

evidence.quote: The dotted line between deceitful and untrustworthy is unexplained. If dotted carries meaning it needs a key; if it carries none it should not look different.
"Some of these words you brought with you. Some are new" is good, but the screen does not show which is which — all six nodes are styled identically.
Style the words the student brought with them differently from the new ones, so the line about it is true on screen.
